To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
driving is associated with activity in a common network of premotor, posterior parietal, cerebellar regions that are also recruited during the preparation of actions.

driving behaviour in a naturalistic environment is associated with activity in a network of brain regions that includes the pre-SMA, premotor, lateral occipito-parietal and cerebello-thalamocortical circuits, and that these regions are differentially engaged by the various aspects of driving behaviour, such as planning, prepared and hazardous actions, as well as monitoring the environment and other road users, and following traffic rules.
driving a vehicle is an everyday behaviour supported by a distributed neural system that includes regions of the premotor cortex, parietal cortex and the cerebellar cortex.

driving behaviour involves a complex interaction of multiple cognitive systems that are supported by a distributed neural network.

there is no one area of the brain that is responsible for all driving behaviours, rather it is a combination of areas that work together in order for us to successfully drive a vehicle in a busy city.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

driving is an extremely complex and dynamic behaviour that is supported by a network of brain regions that is more extensive than previously thought and that is recruited on a moment-by-moment basis to support the many different events that comprise driving.
the neural substrates of driving are complex and dynamic, and depend on the demands of the environment.
we identified a network of brain regions that underpin the different cognitive components that are required to drive a vehicle safely and efficiently.

the brain is highly flexible and can rapidly reconfigure its activity in order to meet the demands of a complex and dynamic task such as driving.
driving is not just an action but a complex cognitive task.
driving in the natural environment is a dynamic process, involving a range of cognitive functions that are supported by different brain systems.
